keywords.term: geographically and temporally neural network weighted regression

div.p: Geographically weighted regression (GWR) and geographically and temporally weighted regression (GTWR) are classic methods for estimating non-stationary relationships. Although these methods have been widely used in geographical modeling and spatiotemporal analysis, they face challenges in adequately expressing spacetime proximity and constructing a kernel with optimal weights. This probably results in an insufficient estimation of spatiotemporal non-stationarity. To address complex non-linear interactions between time and space, a spatiotemporal proximity neural network (STPNN) is proposed in this paper to accurately generate space-time distance. A geographically and temporally neural network weighted regression (GTNNWR) model that extends geographically neural network weighted regression (GNNWR) with the proposed STPNN is then developed to effectively model spatiotemporal non-stationary relationships. To examine its performance, we conducted two case studies of simulated datasets and environmental modeling in coastal areas of Zhejiang, China. The GTNNWR model was fully evaluated by comparing with ordinary linear regression (OLR), GWR, GNNWR, and GTWR models. The results demonstrated that GTNNWR not only achieved the best fitting and prediction performance but also exactly quantified spatiotemporal non-stationary relationships. Further, GTNNWR has the potential to handle complex spatiotemporal non-stationarity in various geographical processes and environmental phenomena.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Spatiotemporal non-stationarity is an intrinsic attribute of most geographical processes, and its estimation is a key issue in modeling spatiotemporal non-stationary relationships. Geographically weighted regression (GWR) is a classic method for estimating spatial nonstationarity that allows the relationship to vary across space (Brunsdon et al. 1996, Fotheringham et al. 2002). Because it can capture spatial non-stationarity in relationships, GWR has been widely used in numerous fields, such as environmental modeling (Zhang et al. 2016, 2019, Zhai et al. 2018, Yang et al. 2019), public health (Chen et al. 2016, Wang et al. 2016, Ge et al. 2017), housing price analysis (Harris et al. 2013, Lu et al. 2016, Cao et al. 2019, Fang et al. 2019), transport geography (Selby and Kockelman 2013, Li et al. 2016, Xu et al. 2019), and crime researches (Cahill andMulligan 2007, Stein et al. 2016).

The space weight matrix is a key component of GWR and is calculated though a userspecified kernel, such as Gaussian and bi-square functions (Fotheringham et al. 2002). Since the weight kernel of only one bandwidth parameter in traditional GWR cannot estimate the multiscale effects in spatial non-stationary relationships, multiscale geographically weighted regression (MGWR) that extends GWR by allowing the bandwidths to be computed for each covariate has been proposed and the inference methods of MGWR has also been developed (Fotheringham et al. 2017, Li et al. 2020, Yu et al. 2020). In addition, considering that the simple and predefined structure of weight kernels in GWR cannot handle the complex non-linear effects between spatial proximity and nonstationary weights in geographical relationships, we recently proposed a geographically neural network weighted regression (GNNWR) model by integrating a neural network with the linear regression (Wu 2018, Du et al. 2020). Similar to the idea of GWR, GNNWR developed a spatial weighted neural network (SWNN) to accurately calculate the space weight matrix, and then combined it with ordinary linear regression (OLR) to estimate spatial non-stationarity. The results of both simulated experiments and environmental modeling illustrated that GNNWR achieved higher performance than GWR and OLR and better quantified the spatial non-stationary relationship (Du et al. 2020).

In addition to space, time is another basic dimension associated with geographical processes and environmental phenomena. In recent years, quite a few studies have been performed to incorporate temporal effects into the GWR model to explain both temporal and spatial non-stationarity (Huang et al. 2010, Wu et al. 2014, Fotheringham et al. 2015). To calibrate spatiotemporal non-stationarity, defining and measuring the space-time distance is a crucial problem. Given that time and space exhibit different scale effects, Huang et al. (2010) designed a straightforward way of combining spatial and temporal distances into a space-time distance and presented a geographically and temporally weighted regression (GTWR) model. Since Huang et al. (2010) assumed an orthogonal space-time coordination system, Wu et al. (2014) improved it by introducing a space-time angle parameter and defined the space-time distance in a relatively complex form.

The space-time distance defined by GTWR and its extended methods solved the problem of space-time integration to a certain extent, and has been successfully applied in diverse domains with excellent results and decent interpretability (Liu et al. 2017, Du et al. 2018a, Wu et al. 2019, Zeng et al. 2019, Zhou and Lin 2019, Dong et al. 2020). It is clear that the capacities of these techniques to characterize spatiotemporal relationships mainly depends on the formulation complexity of space-time distance. However, the form of space-time distance usually requires a priori assumption and should be assumed to be relatively simple (e.g. linear weighted function) so as to eliminate the estimation problem in the terminal model. This is probably unable to deal with the complex nonlinear interactions caused by multiscale differences between time and space.

In essence, constructing a space-time distance can be regarded as a non-linear fusion of time and space. The neural network has been widely used to tackle non-linear problems and has obtained outstanding achievements in many disciplines (Deng and Yu 2014, LeCun et al. 2015, Schmidhuber 2015). Considering that neural networks have the potential to capture the complex non-linear effects in space-time, this paper proposes a spatiotemporal proximity neural network (STPNN) to accurately generate space-time distance. Making full use of neural networks to fit the space-time distance and nonstationary weight matrix, we extend GNNWR with the proposed STPNN to incorporate temporal effects into spatial non-stationarity and accordingly develop a geographically and temporally neural network weighted regression (GTNNWR) model to estimate spatiotemporal non-stationary relationships.

The remainder is structured as below. The next section defines the STPNN and then specifies the procedure of incorporating STPNN into GNNWR to achieve GTNNWR. In Sections 3 and 4, we present the implementation of GTNNWR through two case studies in which its performance is fully evaluated by comparison with the OLR, GWR, GNNWR, and GTWR models. Finally, the conclusions are given in the last Section.

When applying the GTNNWR model, the significance level of spatiotemporal nonstationarity over the study area should be evaluated first. After constructing the final model, the significance of spatiotemporal variations of each parameter's coefficients should also be examined. Since it is difficult to compute the exact distributions of test statistics for local models, using approximate distributions is a feasible way to tackle model testing problems (Leung et al. 2000). By utilizing the approximate distributions of residual sum of squares and the estimated variance, Du et al. (2020) proposed two tests (F 1 and F 2 ) of the null hypothesis for the diagnosis of GNNWR. These two tests are also available for GTNNWR and are adopted for its diagnosis in this study. In addition, we should point out that the bandwidth parameter in GWR-based (i.e. GWR and GTWR) methods can be used as an indicator of the space-time scale in the estimated relationship. However, the concept of bandwidth is weakened in GNNWR-based methods (i.e. GNNWR and GTNNWR). The non-stationary weights of independent variables in GTNNWR are calculated through the STWNN. Hence, the weight and bias parameters of STWNN are similar to the bandwidth parameter in GTWR, but it is difficult to use them to explain the space-time scale due to the complex mathematical structure of the neural network. In view of this, the explanatory power of model parameters in GTNNWR is somewhat inferior to GTWR. On the other hand, the limited model parameters of GTWR would result in a simple structure of the weight kernel, which cannot handle the complex non-linear effects between spatiotemporal proximity and non-stationary weights (Du et al. 2020). In contrast, by using the non-linear fitting ability of the neural network, GTNNWR can construct an accurate weight kernel (i.e. STWNN) with a sophisticated structure to fully address these problems. Therefore, GTNNWR is capable to achieve higher estimation accuracy of spatiotemporal non-stationarity and obtain more reasonable space-time varying coefficients than GTWR.

div.head: Model design and estimation
div.p: The estimation accuracy of GTNNWR is mainly dependent on the learning capacities of the STPNN and the STWNN, which are integrated to form a deep neural network with multiple hidden layers. To enhance the optimization efficiency of GTNNWR, this paper designs its neural network architecture as shown in Figure 3.

Since the space-time proximity in STPNN is simplified to a space-time distance in this study, the STPNN only integrates spatial distance and temporal distance into a space-time distance, which is simple for neural network modeling. Hence, the STPNN adopts a three-layer architecture, including one input layer, one output layer, and a hidden layer. The input layer is the spatial and temporal distances, and the output layer is a space-time distance. The STWNN adopts a multi-layer architecture, including one input layer, one output layer, and several hidden layers. The input layer is an aggregation of the STPNNs' outputs, and the output layer is the space-time weight matrix. The number of hidden layers in the STWNN is determined by the complexity of the estimated process. In addition, several training techniques are utilized for superior computing power, including Dropout technology (Srivastava et al. 2014), robust parameter initialization method and parametric rectified linear unit (Parametric ReLU) activation function (He et al. 2015), and batch normalization technique (Ioffe and Szegedy 2015).

The implementation procedure of GTNNWR is shown in Figure 4. First, we randomly divide the experimental data into two subsets: training data (including validation data) and testing data. To avoid over-fitting, a 10-fold cross-validation procedure is adopted for model estimation. The training data is split into 10 smaller sets (i.e. 10 folds). Then, the data of 9 folds are used for model training and the remaining fold data is used to validate the obtained model, which is repeated for 10 iterations. When the best model parameters are achieved through the cross-validation procedure, the final evaluation of model performance is performed on the testing data.

div.head: Simulated dataset
div.p: Using simulated datasets with known spatiotemporal non-stationary relationships to evaluate model performance is quite convincing. A simulation process is therefore designed and repeated for 100 realizations to fully examine the performance and robustness of GTNNWR. div.head: Experiment implementation
div.p: Each simulated dataset is randomly divided into training data (85%) and testing data (15%) for experimentation. The training data is used to optimize the model parameters through a 10-fold cross-validation procedure and the testing data is utilized to evaluate the prediction capacity of the optimal model.

Five different models, i.e. OLR, GWR, GNNWR, GTWR and the proposed GTNNWR models, are conducted on the same dataset. For GWR and GTWR, two commonly used kernels, i.e. the fixed Gaussian kernel and adaptive bi-square kernel, are applied for comparison, and the corrected Akaike information criterion (AICc) is used as the performance criterion (Table 1). The GWR and GTWR models are implemented in MATLAB and optimized by the built-in minimization function fminbnd.

The mean square error (MSE) is adopted as the loss function of GNNWR and GTNNWR. The mini-batch stochastic gradient descent algorithm is applied for the parameter optimization of neural networks. A five-layer STWNN architecture that includes one input layer, one output layer, and three hidden layers is adopted for GTNNWR. A simple grid search strategy proposed by Du et al. (2020) is used to determine the neuron sizes of hidden layers. The optimal neural network structures and hyper-parameters of GTNNWR are shown in Table 2. The structure of SWNN of GNNWR is the same as the STWNN of GTNNWR. The GNNWR and GTNNWR models are built using TensorFlow 1.5.0 and Python 3.6.

div.head: Results and discussion
div.p: Table 3 shows the mean performance of spatiotemporal estimations of 100 simulated datasets for the OLR, GWR, GNNWR, GTWR and GTNNWR models. With the consideration of non-stationarity, GWR-based and GNNWR-based models achieve significantly higher performance than OLR for all statistical indicators. Regarding the fitting performance of the 10-fold cross-validation results, the training and validation performance of two GWR models are comparable in terms of R 2 , RMSE, and MAE values. GNNWR obtains lower training accuracy than the GWR models, but its validation accuracy is higher. Comparing the fitting results of two GTWR models, GTWR-AAB is superior to GTWR-AFG for both training and validation. Moreover, the fitting accuracy of GTWR is clearly higher than GWR and GNNWR. For example, the training and validation R 2 values of GWR-AAB are increased from 0.850 and 0.811 to 0.923 and 0.829 of GTWR-AAB, and the training and validation RMSE values are decreased from 0.565 and 0.629 to 0.404 and 0.598, respectively.

Comparing the fitting performance of GTNNWR and GTWR, we can see that although the training accuracy of GTNNWR is slightly higher than GTWR-AAB, its validation accuracy is far superior to GTWR-AAB. Specifically, GTNNWR improves the training R 2 and RMSE of GTWR-AAB from 0.923 and 0.404 to 0.928 and 0.390, while the validation R 2 and RMSE of GTWR-AAB are greatly enhanced from 0.829 and 0.598 to 0.887 and 0.485 of GTNNWR. Moreover, the validation accuracy of GTWR is considerably worse than its training accuracy, suggesting that GTWR encounters somewhat over-fitting.

In addition to the fitting results of training and validation datasets, the prediction performance of the testing dataset is another important measurement for model evaluation. The prediction results of OLR, GWR, GNNWR, GTWR and GTNNWR are also displayed in Table 3. It can be seen that the prediction accuracy differences among the models are similar to the fitting results. The prediction performance of GNNWR is slightly better than GWR but inferior to GTWR. Notably, GTNNWR achieves a much higher prediction accuracy than the other models. GTNNWR increases the prediction R 2 of GTWR-AAB from 0.829 to 0.879, and the prediction RMSE and MAE values of GTWR-AAB are respectively decreased by 16.1% and 17.7%.

Except evaluating the estimation accuracy of the dependent variable, the estimated spatiotemporal relationship (i.e. the space-time varying coefficients) is usually used to conduct inference and prediction. It is important to examine whether the GWR-based and GNNWR-based models indeed quantify the spatiotemporal non-stationary relationships by comparing their estimated coefficients with the pre-simulated coefficients. As shown in Figures 678, the estimated coefficients of GWR and GNNWR do not vary over time because they don't consider temporal non-stationarity while the estimated coefficients of GTWR and GTNNWR shows significant variations over time and space.

More specifically, for β 0 u i ; v i ; t i ð Þ as shown in Figure 6, although GWR and GNNWR do not reflect temporal variations, their spatial distributions are fairly similar to the simulated distribution, indicating that they sufficiently address the spatial non-stationarity. The spatiotemporal distribution of GTWR coefficients shows that its temporal trend is basically consistent with the simulated dataset but its spatial distribution is not quite accurate, even worse than GWR and GNNWR. This demonstrates that although GTWR is endowed the capability to handle both temporal and spatial non-stationarity, its ability to capture spatial non-stationarity is somewhat impaired. In the meantime, the spatiotemporal distribution of GTNNWR coefficients of β 0 u i ; v i ; t i ð Þ agree well with the simulated coefficients, such as the main shape and the details in four corners. This suggests that GTNNWR best captures the spatiotemporal non-stationary characteristics of the simulated relationship. Figure 7 demonstrates that the estimation accuracy of each model is not satisfactory for β 1 u i ; v i ; t i ð Þ, but GTNNWR still performs better than the other models in terms of the spatial distribution and temporal trend. With regard to β 2 u i ; v i ; t i ð Þ, the accuracy difference among the models is similar to that of β 0 u i ; v i ; t i ð Þ as shown in Figure 8. On the whole, GTNNWR and GTWR effectively handle the spatiotemporal variations of β 2 u i ; v i ; t i ð Þ while GNNWR and GWR only clearly reflect the spatial distribution of β 2 u i ; v i ; t i ð Þ. Obviously, the estimation accuracy of GTNNWR for β 2 u i ; v i ; t i ð Þ is still the best. Further, we find that the estimated coefficients of GNNWR-based models exhibit smoother spatial patterns with less noise than those of GWR-based models. This indicates that GNNWR-based models can obtain fairly reasonable distributions of the spatially varying coefficients through the nonlinear fitting of neural networks.

To quantitatively compare the estimation effects of the simulated relationship among these models, the mean values of Pearson's r and RMSE between the estimated coefficients and the simulated coefficients of GWR, GNNWR, GTWR and GTNNWR over 100 simulated datasets are displayed in Table 4. The values of Pearson's r and RMSE presented by the boxplots are also shown in Figure 9. Consistent with our previous analyses, the mean values of Pearson's r and RMSE of GTNNWR are significantly better than the other models and its boxplots also show considerable advantages, further proving its superiority and robustness in the modeling of spatiotemporal non-stationarity. Moreover, it is unexpected that the statistics of Pearson's r and RMSE of GTWR coefficients are slightly worse than GWR, which suggests that GTWR may not be reliable due to its simple form of space-time distance and cannot always adequately handle the spatiotemporal nonstationarity. It is noteworthy that GNNWR obtains better statistical indicators than GWR and GTWR, suggesting that GNNWR effectively captures the complex non-stationary features by using its SWNN (Wu et al. 2020). In summary, GTNNWR not only achieves the best estimation performance but also sufficiently characterizes the spatiotemporal non-stationary features in the simulated relationship. These results also indicate that the STPNN successfully addresses the complex non-linear interactions of time and space and is more effective than the space-time distance of GTWR.

In addition, it should be noted that the model complexity of GTNNWR is considerably higher than GTWR. Nonetheless, the structure of GTNNWR with several hidden layers (usually < 10) is quite simple compared with the diverse models in the fields of neural networks and deep learning, so its training efficiency can be pretty high. The optimal GTNNWR model is usually achievable within 10-15 minutes in our experiments since it can easily take advantage of powerful parallel computational capabilities of GPU units and distributed computing systems by using machine learning frameworks (e.g. TensorFlow). Further, the model complexity does not significantly raise with the rapid growth of data amount, so the efficiency of GTNNWR will still be acceptable for big data. On the other hand, although GTWR built in the CPU environment achieves higher efficiency (3-5 minutes) than GTNNWR, its efficiency may rapidly decrease when the data amount increases due to its inability to use parallel computational capabilities of the hardware. In view of the great superiority of GTNNWR in modeling spatiotemporal non-stationarity as illustrated in our experiments, the training complexity and computational efficiency of GTNNWR are generally acceptable for most geographical processes.

div.head: Study area and dataset
div.p: The study area is located in the Zhejiang coastal areas (ZCA) of the East China Sea as shown in Figure 10. Algal bloom is one of the main ecological disasters in the spring of ZCA and has caused serious damages to the development of Zhejiang Province (Zhang et al. 2017, Jiang et al. 2019). Many studies have shown that the algal bloom is strongly associated with marine physical, chemical and biological factors (Qin et al. 2017, Du et al. 2018b). To interpret the evolution of algal bloom in ZCA, it is important to understand the interactions between various environmental parameters. This paper intends to use GTNNWR to quantify the spatiotemporal non-stationary relationship between algal bloom indicator and environmental parameters to help reveal the underlying mechanism of algal blooms in ZCA.

Water quality data collected in the spring of 2013-2017 in ZCA are used for experiments. The total dataset consists of 1461 observations and their spatial distribution in each year is somewhat different. The station distribution in 2017 is presented in Figure 10. The experimental dataset offers a number of water quality parameters, including pH, models, the fixed Gaussian kernel and adaptive bi-square kernel are applied for comparison as shown in Table 1. The optimal neural network structures and hyper-parameter settings of GTNNWR are presented in Table 6. The structure of SWNN in GNNWR is the same as the STWNN of GTNNWR.

div.head: Model performance
div.p: Table 7 shows the performance indicators of the OLR, GWR, GNNWR, GTWR and GTNNWR models for the spatiotemporal estimation of Chl-a in the spring of ZCA over 2013-2017. For the 10-fold cross-validation results, we can note that both GWR and GNNWR are considerably better than OLR for all statistical indicators. The F 1 test values of the GWRbased and GNNWR-based models also demonstrate that the relationship between Chl-a and the explanatory parameters is significantly non-stationary over time and space.

In addition, the performance of GNNWR is superior to GWR-AFG but inferior to GWR-AAB in terms of R 2 , RMSE, and MAE values for model training. The validation accuracy of GNNWR is better than two GWR models. Comparing the fitting results of two GTWR models, GTWR-AAB is considerably better than GTWR-AFG for both training and validation. Moreover, the fitting accuracy of GTWR-AAB is also superior to GWR and GNNWR, demonstrating that GTWR-AAB is capable of dealing with spatiotemporal nonstationarity. It can also be observed that the fitting results of GWR-based models with adaptive kernel (i.e. GWR-AAB and GTWR-AAB) are superior to the corresponding models with fixed kernel (i.e. GWR-AFG and GTWR-AFG), suggesting that the right choice of weight kernel is crucial to the GWR-based models.

The fitting results in Table 7 also reveal that the statistical indicators of GTNNWR are much better than those of the GWR, GNNWR and GTWR models. Compared to the best comparison model, GTNNWR significantly improves the training and validation R 2 of GTWR-AAB from 0.843 and 0.568 to 0.915 and 0.728, respectively. The training and validation RMSE values of GTWR-AAB are decreased from 4.230 and 6.692 to 3.107 and 5.306 of GTNNWR (both declines exceed 20%). The training and validation MAE values of GTWR-AAB are also reduced by 18.6% and 14.5%, respectively. These results indicate that extending GNNWR with the STPNN greatly improves the fitting performance of the spatiotemporal non-stationary relationship of Chl-a in coastal environments. Further, we find that GTWR-AAB achieves a fitting performance comparable to GTNNWR in the simulation experiment, but its fitting performance is much worse than GTNNWR in this environment modeling. This is mainly because the spatiotemporal non-linear interactions in the real geographical process are more complex than in the simulation process. GTWR-AAB is difficult to effectively capture these complex spatiotemporal non-linear interactions due to its simple form of space-time distance and weight kernel.

In addition, the prediction results of the OLR, GWR, GNNWR, GTWR and GTNNWR models for the testing dataset are also shown in Table 7. We can see that although the statistical indicators of OLR for prediction is still the worst among all the models, its prediction performance is even better than its fitting performance. This indicates that OLR does not suffer from over-fitting. Comparing the prediction performance among the GWR, GNNWR and GTWR models, it is unexpected that GTWR-AAB with the best fitting accuracy acquired the worst prediction accuracy among these models. In contrast, the GTWR-AFG model with poor fitting accuracy has obtained the best prediction accuracy. This finding suggests that GTWR is not very stable and possibly encounter severe over-fitting. Moreover, we note that GTWR also suffer from over-fitting in the simulation experiment but much lighter than in environmental modeling, indicating that the simple structure of weight kernel and the simple form of space-time distance in GTWR cannot correctly handle the complex non-stationary features in real geographical processes. It is worth noting that the prediction accuracy of GTNNWR is notably higher than the other models. For instance, the prediction R 2 of GTWR-AFG is increased from 0.601 to 0.681 for GTNNWR, and the prediction RMSE and MAE values of GTWR-AFG are respectively decreased by 10.6% and 11.7%.

In the following analysis, GWR-AAB and GTWR-AAB with superior performance are selected as the representative of GWR and GTWR. To further compare the performance among these models, the estimated Chl-a values (including training, validation, and testing datasets) versus the observed Chl-a values are portrayed as scatter plots in Figure 11. The scatter plots of OLR are more dispersed than the other models, which is consistent with its worst performance. It can be noted that GWR and GNNWR have relatively high accuracy for estimating low values, but commonly underestimate high values. For the GTWR model, its estimates for training and validation show much higher fitting accuracy than GWR and GNNWR, but its estimates for the testing dataset present an even worse distribution than GWR and GNNWR due to its over-fitting. Obviously, we can see that the estimates of GTNNWR show the highest fitting and prediction precision and rarely encounter unreasonable underestimates and overestimates. Similar to the experimental results of simulated datasets, GTNNWR also achieves the best fitting and prediction performance for modeling the spatiotemporal non-stationary relationship between Chl-a and environmental parameters.

div.head: Diagnosis of spatiotemporal non-stationarity
div.p: The F 1 test values of the GWR, GNNWR, GTWR and GTNNWR models in Table 7 demonstrate that the relationship between Chl-a and pH, DO, COD, and PO 4 , in the spring of ZCA is characterized with significant spatiotemporal non-stationarity as a whole. To further investigate whether each set of parameters varies notably, F 2 tests are conducted on the coefficients of each parameter for these models (Table 8). It can be noted that the significance level of each parameter for all models reaches 0.01, suggesting that the estimated relationship not only presents significant spatiotemporal non-stationarity overall but also exhibits distinct non-stationary features for each parameter. Moreover, the F 2 test values of GTNNWR are considerably higher than the other models, further confirming that GTNNWR accurately estimates the spatiotemporal non-stationary relationship.

div.head: Spatiotemporal non-stationary relationship between Chl-a and environmental parameters
div.p: Similar to GWR-based models, we can analyse the GTNNWR coefficients to further explore the spatiotemporal non-stationary relationship between Chl-a and environmental parameters in the spring of ZCA. As shown in Table 9, we can see that the parameter coefficients of GWR, GNNWR, GTWR and GTNNWR include both positive and negative values, suggesting that the impacts of water quality parameters on Chl-a may present opposite effects at different positions or at different times.

The local estimates of GTNNWR are viewable over time and space. To study the quantitative space-time association between Chl-a and the selected parameters in the spring of ZCA, the spatiotemporal variations of Chl-a and the GTNNWR coefficients of each parameter are mapped in Figure 12. We can see that the spatial distribution of Chl-a greatly varies in the spring of ZCA during 2013-2017. The high concentration of Chl-a mainly occurs in the northern areas of ZCA, which may be the main reason for the frequent algal blooms in these sea areas in spring (Ye et al. 2017, Wu et al. 2020). Overall, the Chl-a concentration in 2017 is lower than in other years, indicating better water quality. In addition, significant spatiotemporal variations of the parameter coefficients are noticed and several space-time varying patterns also exhibit. The pH manifests positive effects on Chl-a as a whole and shows more dramatic influence in the nearshore than the offshore. In addition, the positive effects of pH on Chl-a greatly increase from 2013 to 2014 and then gradually decrease from 2015 to 2017. The DO also basically exhibits positive impacts on Chl-a in ZCA over 2013-2017 and its impacts steadily increase from 2013 to 2016 and abruptly decline in 2017. The space-time varying pattern of the COD is similar to that of the pH, which also presents stronger positive impacts in the nearshore than the offshore and reaches the greatest impacts in 2014. As for the PO 4 , it mainly shows negative effects on Chl-a in the northern ZCA and positive effects on Chl-a in the southern ZCA. The negative impacts of PO 4 on Chl-a achieve the highest in 2014, while the positive impacts reach the greatest in 2015. Moreover, we find that the spatiotemporal patterns of Chl-a and pH coefficients are quite similar, suggesting that the sea areas with greater pH influence is likely to cause high concentration of Chl-a. Meanwhile, the effects of DO and COD are found to be relatively great in high Chl-a areas, such as the northern areas of ZCA in 2014 and 2016. This indicates that the larger discharges of DO and COD is probably the main cause of the high concentration of Chla in 2014 and 2016. Through the GTNNWR modeling, we explicitly quantify the spatiotemporal non-stationary relationship between Chl-a and environmental parameters. These results are conducive to explain the main drivers of algal blooms and also suggest that the spatiotemporal changes of Chl-a may be controllable by managing different parameters in the certain areas in the spring of ZCA (Du et al. 2018a, Wu et al. 2020).

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: In this study, an STPNN is constructed to address the complex non-linear interactions between time and space to accurately generate space-time distance. A geo-statistical method named GTNNWR, which extends GNNWR with the STPNN, is then proposed to effectively perform the estimation of spatiotemporal non-stationarity. The proposed GTNNWR model has the potential to handle spatiotemporal non-stationary relationships in various geographical processes and environmental phenomena. Two case studies of simulated datasets and environmental modeling show that GTNNWR has achieved the best fitting and prediction performance compared to the OLR, GWR, GNNWR, and GTWR models according to multiple statistical indicators, such as R 2 , RMSE, and MAE values. The simulation experiment further demonstrates that GTNNWR sufficiently captures the spatiotemporal non-stationary features and exactly quantifies the simulated relationship. It can also be concluded that the STPNN adequately addresses the complex non-linear interactions of time and space and is more effective than the space-time distance of GTWR. In addition, we quantitatively clarify the spatiotemporal relationship between Chl-a and environmental parameters through the modeling of GTNNWR, which is conducive to understand the underlying mechanism of algal blooms in ZCA.

It should also be pointed out that although GTNNWR has an excellent estimation capacity, its computational efficiency is not as good as GTWR. GTNNWR is more suitable for modeling complex spatiotemporal non-stationary relationships, but for simple and fast estimations, GTWR can achieve comparable performance and higher efficiency of GTNNWR, which will be a better choice. Several limitations should also be addressed in the future. First, the STPNN is simplified by considering only a special case where its output length is one. Complex neural networks should be considered and examined to better capture the non-linear interactions of time and space. Second, it is still difficult to interpret the obtained weighed neural network in GNNWR-based methods, so we will further explore the structure of the weighted neural network and try to understand its mechanism.
